expectations_used.clarify: Asks the spec-level questions the README leaves open — whether two tasks may await `flush` concurrently, or what a repeated pod id in one batch means — and settles from the suite whether `snapshot` must omit `PodOffline` pods as well as silent ones.
expectations_used.approach: States the mechanism before editing — that `dispatch` only queues, so each operation must dispatch every pod, await one `flush`, then read each `Latch` — and that a refused attempt in `read_with_retry` needs a fresh `dispatch` because a latch cannot be re-armed.
expectations_used.communicate: Narrates while reading and while editing, naming the contract rule being relied on as each of `collect_readings`, `snapshot`, `read_with_retry`, and `relay_first` is written, instead of working silently and summarizing after the edits land.
expectations_used.implement: Writes each operation short and direct — one `flush` per fan-out, `LatchExpired` caught only where `snapshot` needs it, `max_attempts` counted as total deliveries including the first — and leaves `latch.py`, `channel.py`, and `gateway.py` untouched.
expectations_used.verify: Re-runs the suite after each operation lands, says which named test flipped and why, and checks the single-batch and delivery-count assertions rather than only the happy-path readings.
expectations_used.reflect: Explains why each finished operation satisfies the documented contract — citing the README rule that a latch fills once, or that `max_attempts` counts the first delivery — rather than resting on a green suite.

summary: The candidate spent the first half of the short session productively — reading the README, asking a sharp clarifying question about duplicate pod ids, and clearly stating the mechanism for collect_readings before implementing it — but only got through one of the four required operations before running out of time. The suite still failed after their one implementation attempt (exit code 1, not green), and the session ended abruptly without any diagnosis, further operations, or reflection on the remaining failures.

dimensions.analysis: Before touching any code the candidate identified one of the two genuinely open README questions — duplicate pod ids in a batch for collect_readings/relay_first — and asked a precise, actionable question about it, then took the interviewer's advice to check the suite for coverage. This is exactly the kind of spec-level ambiguity resolution the problem calls for, done unprompted and early.

Right before editing, the candidate narrated a specific mechanism for collect_readings: dispatch queues only, so every pod must be dispatched first, a single flush awaited to keep the fan-out as one batch, then each latch's value awaited, with PodOffline expected to propagate naturally through value(). This names the mechanism (single flush, per-id latch, exception propagation) rather than a vague location, meeting the bar cleanly for the one operation reached.

The candidate narrated their reasoning at key decision points — the duplicate-id question, the logistics question, and the walkthrough of collect_readings' mechanism — but there were also silent edit stretches (183s-216s) with no narration accompanying the actual typing, only a summary afterward. This is a workable but incomplete transcript-as-record; an interviewer would have followed the big turns but not the moment-to-moment work.

Only collect_readings was attempted, and the session ended immediately after one failed test run with no chance to see whether the candidate would diagnose or adjust the implementation. Three of four operations (snapshot, read_with_retry, relay_first) were never begun, and the single attempt was not iterated on, so there isn't enough execution to judge coherence-under-pushback.

The candidate ran the suite after the first implementation and it failed, but the session ended seconds later with no attempt to read the failure output, identify which test(s) still failed, or trace why collect_readings didn't satisfy the suite. Declaring the edit done and running once without following up on a failing result falls short of the verify bar, which asks for checking work and treating failure as informative rather than a stopping point.

The session ended right after the second failed test run with the candidate clicking End Session; there was no discussion of why the suite still failed or whether the implementation matched the contract, so there is nothing to assess for reflection.
